title: When the net wins
objectives: Build a simulated panel where a network beats boosting, and name the data shapes that cause it.

screens.title: Two signals
screens.prose: This lesson takes about fifteen minutes; interview pace is five minutes a question. Two simulated worlds, 150 stock-days each. Left, world A's signal against one feature: steps. Right, world B's signal against a diagonal combination of all eight features: smooth.
screens.question: Which world should favour the network?

options.text: World B: a smooth signal along an oblique direction.
World A: its jumps need a flexible model.
options.why: Jumps on one feature are exactly what a tree split fits.

options.text: Neither: trees win on any tabular data.
options.why: On world B the network wins on both seeds; the shape of the signal decides.

hints.text: How does a tree cut the feature space?
One feature at a time, at a threshold.
A smooth diagonal needs many steps; a network fits it directly.

feedback.correct: Smooth and oblique favours the network.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how each model bends.

byKey.A: A threshold on one feature is a single tree split.

explain.text: World A is two thresholds on two of eight features, with heavy-tailed noise. World B is smooth along a diagonal of all eight, which costs a tree many small steps.

screens.prose: The same three models and the same split as l10, on world B. Slide between the seeds.
screens.question: On seed 0, by how much does the network's $R^2$ beat boosting's? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Subtract boosting's bar from the network's.

feedback.correct: $0.0055$: the network leads in world B.

byKey.ridge: That is the network over ridge.

explain.text: The network leads by $0.0055$ on seed 0 and $0.0027$ on seed 1. Whether that is real is l10's question.

screens.title: Is it real?
screens.prose: The paired daily differences for world B seed 0 have mean $-0.0233$ and standard error $0.0068$.
screens.question: What is $t$? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Mean over standard error.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by its standard error.

byKey.sign: Network minus boosting is negative here: the network wins.

explain.text: $t = -3.45$ is beyond $-2$, so on seed 0 the network's lower error is unlikely to be chance.

options.text: Same direction, not significant alone: the evidence leans to the network but needs more seeds or data.
The network's seed 0 win was luck; keep the trees.
options.why: Seed 1 agrees in sign; it is weak evidence, not contrary evidence.

options.text: Switch to the network now.
options.why: One significant seed and one weak one is not yet the bar you set.

hints.text: Is $|t|$ above 2 on seed 1?
Same sign, weaker: gather more evidence.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read both the sign and the size of $t$.

byKey.reject: A weak result in the same direction is not evidence against.

explain.text: Seed 0 says $t = -3.45$, seed 1 $-1.91$. Same sign, one significant: a decision waits for more seeds or a longer test.

screens.title: One seed as a rule
screens.prose: A colleague saw world B seed 0 ($t = -3.45$) and writes: "Networks beat trees on smooth signals. Rule established."
screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: One seed is one draw of the data; seed 1 was not significant.
Nothing: $|t| > 2$ settles it.
options.why: For that draw only. Seed 1 gives $t = -1.91$.

options.text: Networks never beat trees.
options.why: They do here on both seeds in $R^2$; the claim is too strong, not wrong in sign.

hints.text: What changes between seeds?
The whole panel: features, signal direction, noise.
A rule needs to survive redraws.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a second draw showed.

byKey.right: Significance on one draw is not a rule across draws.

explain.text: A seed redraws the panel and the signal's direction. A finding that holds on one seed and fades on the next is a hypothesis, not a rule.

screens.title: Ridge beats boosting
screens.prose: Edge case: on world B seed 1, even ridge beats the trees.
screens.question: By how much does ridge's $R^2$ beat boosting's? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Ridge minus boosting.

feedback.correct: $0.0023$: a smooth signal rewards a smooth model.

byKey.sign: Ridge is the higher bar here.

explain.text: Ridge, a straight line, beats the trees by $0.0023$ here: much of world B's signal is close to linear in $u$. Steps are a costly way to draw a slope.

screens.title: The shapes, aloud
screens.prose: The spoken list: networks tend to win with smooth signals along combinations of features, with many assets sharing structure (one model, an asset embedding), and with sequences or text. Trees tend to win with thresholds, many useless features and heavy tails. $$\text{shape of the signal} \Rightarrow \text{model}$$
screens.question: Which data favour the trees? Select all that apply.

options.text: Signals that switch at a level of one feature.
Many uninformative features.
Heavy-tailed noise.
News text as an input.
options.why: Text needs learned representations; networks are the natural model.

options.text: A smooth signal along a mix of all features.
options.why: That is world B, where the network won.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what single-feature splits do well.

explain.text: Single-feature splits ignore useless inputs and are robust to outliers. A smooth oblique signal or a text input plays to a network instead.

screens.title: 3,000 stocks and text
screens.prose: A fund forecasts returns for 3,000 stocks, with 40 numeric features and the day's news headlines for each stock.
screens.question: Where would you try a network first?

options.text: On the headlines, with a shared model across stocks, compared with trees on the numeric features alone.
On the 40 numeric features alone, replacing the trees.
options.why: That is where trees are strongest; the text is where a network adds something new.

options.text: One network per stock.
options.why: Each stock has too little data; sharing one model across stocks is the network's strength.

hints.text: Which input do trees handle worst?
Raw text.
A shared network on the text, tested against the trees.

feedback.correct: Text and shared structure favour the network.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Where do trees struggle?

explain.text: Trees need hand-made features from text; a network learns them, and one model across 3,000 stocks has plenty of data. Test it with the same paired comparison.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge


def small_panel_compare(world, seed, assets, days):
    X, y, sig = panel(world, seed, assets, days)
    n_test = days * 3 // 10
    n_tr = days - n_test
    Xtr, ytr = X[:n_tr].reshape(-1, X.shape[2]), y[:n_tr].ravel()
    Xte, yte = X[n_tr:].reshape(-1, X.shape[2]), y[n_tr:].ravel()
    sst = np.sum((yte - yte.mean()) ** 2)
    r2 = lambda p: float(1 - np.sum((yte - p) ** 2) / sst)
    models = {
        'boost': HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_leaf_nodes=15, random_state=0),
        'mlp': MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(32, 32), alpha=1e-3, max_iter=300, early_stopping=True, random_state=0),
        'ridge': Ridge(alpha=1.0),
    }
    out = {k: r2(m.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)) for k, m in models.items()}
    out['oracle'] = r2(sig[n_tr:].ravel())
    return out
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np


def panel(world, seed, assets=100, days=500, p=8):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((days, assets, p))
    if world == 'A':
        sig = 0.6 * ((X[..., 0] > 0.8).astype(float) - (X[..., 1] < -0.8).astype(float)) * ((X[..., 0] > 0.8) | (X[..., 1] < -0.8))
        sig = sig + 0.4 * (X[..., 0] > 0.8) * (X[..., 1] > 0.5)
        noise = rng.standard_t(3, (days, assets)) / np.sqrt(3)
    else:
        w = rng.standard_normal(p)
        w /= np.linalg.norm(w)
        u = X @ w
        v = X @ np.roll(w, 3)
        sig = 0.5 * np.tanh(1.5 * u) + 0.15 * u * v
        noise = rng.standard_normal((days, assets))
    y = sig + 5.0 * noise * np.std(sig)
    return X, y, sig

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge


def small_panel_compare(world, seed, assets, days):
    X, y, sig = panel(world, seed, assets, days)
    n_test = days * 3 // 10
    n_tr = days - n_test
    idx = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(days)
    Xtr, ytr = X[idx[:n_tr]].reshape(-1, X.shape[2]), y[idx[:n_tr]].ravel()
    Xte, yte = X[idx[n_tr:]].reshape(-1, X.shape[2]), y[idx[n_tr:]].ravel()
    sst = np.sum((yte - yte.mean()) ** 2)
    r2 = lambda p: float(1 - np.sum((yte - p) ** 2) / sst)
    models = {
        'boost': HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_leaf_nodes=15, random_state=0),
        'mlp': MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(32, 32), alpha=1e-3, max_iter=300, early_stopping=True, random_state=0),
        'ridge': Ridge(alpha=1.0),
    }
    out = {k: r2(m.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)) for k, m in models.items()}
    out['oracle'] = r2(sig[n_tr:].ravel())
    return out

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer goes on: "How would you make the trees catch up on world B?"
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: Add rotated features, such as a few principal components or random projections.
Allow deeper trees or more rounds, with early stopping.
Start boosting from a linear model, or add one as a base learner.
Drop half the features at random.
options.why: That removes signal; world B's signal uses all eight features.

options.text: Use fewer, shallower trees.
options.why: That makes the staircase coarser, the opposite of what a smooth slope needs.

hints.text: What does a tree lack on a smooth diagonal?
The direction, and the slope.
Rotated inputs, finer steps, a linear base.

feedback.correct: Give the trees the diagonal, more steps, or a linear start.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does a tree lack on a smooth diagonal?

explain.text: Trees lack the oblique direction and the slope. Rotated inputs give them the direction, more depth gives finer steps, and a linear base gives the slope.

ideas: With a smooth, oblique signal the network wins: world B seed 0 $0.0386$ against $0.0331$, $t = -3.45$.
One seed is not a rule: seed 1 has the same sign but $t = -1.91$.
Networks: smooth oblique signals, shared structure, text. Trees: thresholds, useless features, heavy tails.
summary.trap: Reading one seed's significant win as a general rule.

quiz.question: A signal is $0.3$ when a stock's momentum rank is in the top decile and 0 otherwise. Which model's bias suits it?

options.text: Trees: one split at the decile.
A network: it is smooth.
options.why: A jump at one level is not smooth; a single split fits it.

options.text: Ridge: it is linear.
options.why: A step is not linear in the rank.

feedback.correct: A threshold is a tree split.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Is the signal smooth or a step?

explain.text: The signal jumps at one level of one feature, exactly what a tree split represents.

quiz.question: World B: seed 0 gives $t = -3.45$, seed 1 $t = -1.91$. How many of the two seeds clear $|t| > 2$?

explain.text: $|-3.45| > 2$ but $|-1.91| < 2$: one of two seeds is significant.

quiz.question: Why can ridge beat boosting on a smooth signal?

options.text: Much of a smooth signal is close to linear, which ridge fits in one step.
Ridge has more parameters than boosting.
options.why: It has fewer: one per feature.

options.text: Only by luck.
options.why: It happens because the signal is nearly linear in parts, not by chance alone.

feedback.generic: Not quite. What shape does ridge fit?

explain.text: A tree draws a slope as a staircase and needs many steps for it; ridge draws it exactly.
